q: How much of what you experience did you actually choose to notice?
g: James treats attention as the faculty that selects, from the blooming confusion of the world, which parts become experience at all. 'My experience is what I agree to attend to.' Attention is not a spotlight on a given world; it is the editor of the world you get.
p: For one hour, note each time the object of your attention changes, and what moved it — your choice, or a stimulus.

q: Where does the mind go when it leaves?
g: A review of the mind-wandering literature: the default state of an unconstrained mind is not blankness but self-generated thought — often about the past, the future, and the self. It is frequent, and it costs both task performance and, in the studies that measure it, mood.
p: Next time you catch yourself far from the task, write the destination: past, future, self, or other.

q: Is a wandering mind an unhappy mind?
w: A Wandering Mind Is an Unhappy Mind
g: Experience-sampling app, ~250,000 reports from 2,250 adults: minds wandered in 46.9% of sampled moments, and people were less happy when wandering than when focused — including when wandering to pleasant topics. The causal direction is contested; the association is large and replicated in later samples.
p: Three times tomorrow, record what you are doing and whether your mind is on it. Compare the two columns at night.

q: What is the brain doing when you are doing nothing?
w: A default mode of brain function
g: A set of midline and parietal regions is more active at rest than during goal-directed tasks. The 'default mode' — later tied to self-reference, memory and future simulation — reframed rest as activity, not absence. The network is well established; its functional interpretation is still argued.
p: Sit for five minutes with no input and note what the mind produces unprompted. That content is the network's output.

q: When does attention stop feeling like effort?
w: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience
g: From experience-sampling studies: absorption is highest when challenge slightly exceeds skill, goals are clear and feedback is immediate. The phenomenology is widely recognised; 'flow' as a measured construct is looser than its popularity suggests, and the challenge-skill model is not precisely specified.
p: Name the last task where time distorted. Rate its challenge and your skill from 1 to 10.

q: Do you know why you did that?
w: Telling More Than We Can Know
g: In a series of experiments, people confidently reported causes of their own judgments that could not have been operative — they confabulated, and did not notice. Verbal reports on higher mental processes are unreliable as causal accounts, though they remain useful as reports of the experience itself.
p: Recall a recent strong preference. Write the reason. Then write one reason that would also explain it and that you cannot rule out.

q: Which parts of you do other people know better than you do?
w: Who Knows What About a Person? The SOKA Model
g: The self–other knowledge asymmetry model: you have privileged access to your internal states (anxiety, intention, self-esteem), but others are often more accurate about evaluable, externally visible traits — intelligence, attractiveness, extraversion, conscientiousness. Neither vantage point dominates; they see different things.
p: Pick one trait you are confident about. Ask two people who know you well to rate it 1–10. Note the gap without arguing with it.

q: Why do you trust your own introspection more than anyone else's?
w: Perception and Misperception of Bias in Human Judgment
g: The introspection illusion: for your own mind you have direct access and therefore trust what you find; for others you have only behaviour, and therefore infer bias. The asymmetry makes you a poor judge of your own biases and a harsh judge of others'.
p: Name a bias you readily see in someone else. Write the last time it operated in you, in the same terms.

q: How clearly defined is your sense of who you are?
w: Self-Concept Clarity: Measurement, Personality Correlates, and Cultural Boundaries
g: Self-concept clarity — how clearly, consistently and stably you hold beliefs about yourself — is measurable and varies widely. Low clarity goes with rumination, neuroticism and lower wellbeing; it is a property of the self-model, not a verdict on the person.
p: Write five statements beginning 'I am'. Note which ones you would still endorse in a year.

q: Is there an owner behind the experiences, or only the series?
g: Parfit argues for reductionism about personal identity: what exists is a chain of experiences, memories and dispositions, not a further fact of 'me' that owns them. The argument is philosophical, not empirical, but it sets the question the empirical work keeps circling: which of your self-descriptions survive scrutiny?
p: Describe yourself without using any noun that implies a fixed essence. Note what is left.

q: Does naming a feeling change it?
w: Knowing What You're Feeling and Knowing What to Do About It
g: People differ in how finely they distinguish emotional states — 'bad' versus 'irritated, disappointed, and tired'. Higher differentiation predicts better emotion regulation, less binge drinking and less aggression. Granularity appears to be a skill, not a fixed trait.
p: Next unpleasant feeling, name it with three candidate words instead of one. Keep the one that fits best.

q: Is emotion in the event or in the body's model of it?
w: Interoceptive Inference, Emotion, and the Embodied Self
g: Emotion can be framed as the brain's inference about the cause of its own bodily signals — a prediction, corrected by input, rather than a readout. This makes emotion partly constructed and partly embodied, and explains why the same arousal can be labelled fear or excitement depending on context.
p: Find your pulse now. Note the story you would tell about that sensation if you did not know its cause.

q: How wrong are you about how long something will hurt?
g: People systematically overestimate the intensity and duration of future emotional reactions. A central cause is immune neglect: we underestimate the mind's capacity to rationalise, reframe and recover. The error is robust across events, including ones people have experienced before.
p: Recall a past event you expected to devastate you. Write how long you expected it to last and how long it did.

q: Is it better to change the situation or to suppress the reaction?
g: Reappraisal — reinterpreting what an event means before the response runs — reduces negative experience with little physiological cost. Suppression — inhibiting the expression after the response has begun — reduces visible expression but leaves or raises physiological arousal and impairs memory for the interaction.
p: Before the next provocation, write one alternative meaning of the event. Then respond.

q: Do you want the wants you have?
w: Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person
g: A person is distinguished not by having desires but by having desires about those desires. Freedom of the will is the alignment of first-order impulses with second-order endorsement — you can act on an urge you disown, and that is the shape of unfreedom.
p: Name one urge you acted on this week that you would not endorse on reflection. That gap is the thing to measure.

q: Why does deciding fail where a plan succeeds?
w: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta-Analysis
g: Across 94 studies, if-then plans ('if situation X arises, I will do Y') raise goal attainment with a medium-to-large effect, d ≈ 0.65. The mechanism is cue-triggered automaticity: the decision is made in advance, so it does not have to be won again at the moment of action.
p: Write one if-then plan for tomorrow: 'If [time/place/cue], then I will [specific act].'

q: How much of your behaviour is character, and how much is situation?
g: Doris reads the social-psychology record — bystander effects, Good Samaritan studies, mood and helping — as evidence that behaviour is highly situation-sensitive and that global character traits predict weakly across contexts. The claim is contested; the narrow point, that context moves behaviour more than people expect, is well supported.
p: Name a trait you claim. Then name the situation in which you reliably do not show it.

q: Does willpower run out like a battery?
w: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect
g: Twenty-three labs, preregistered protocol, 2,141 participants: the ego-depletion effect was d = 0.04 and not distinguishable from zero. The 'willpower as a depletable resource' story that dominated self-control writing for two decades did not replicate under controlled conditions.
p: Notice where you explain a failure as 'no willpower left'. Substitute one situational explanation and one planning explanation.
